common_name: The Alnwick Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; The Alnwick Rose's compact, rounded habit fits a smaller border position than many other David Austin cultivars.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001 and named for Alnwick Garden in Northumberland, The Alnwick Rose bears rich rose-pink, cupped rosette flowers with a strong, sweet old-rose fragrance, on a compact, rounded, well-branched shrub that fits smaller borders more easily than larger English rose cultivars. It repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost, and its dependable habit and strong fragrance have made it a long-standing favorite in David Austin's catalog.
sources: David Austin Roses — The Alnwick Rose variety notes

common_name: The Pilgrim Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since The Pilgrim is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber against a wall, fence, or pillar.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1991, The Pilgrim carries soft, clear yellow, deeply cupped rosette flowers with a strong myrrh fragrance, on long, arching canes that reach 8 feet or more when trained as a climber, or can be kept pruned as a large freestanding shrub. It was one of the earlier David Austin introductions to combine a strong yellow color with reliable repeat bloom and good disease resistance, and it continues to flower generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Princess Alexandra of Kent Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Princess Alexandra of Kent's fragrance intensifies as each bloom ages, so established, well-fed plants tend to be the most fragrant.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2007, Princess Alexandra of Kent produces rich, pure pink, cupped rosette flowers with a fresh tea fragrance that grows stronger as each bloom matures, on a vigorous, healthy, well-branched shrub with glossy, disease-resistant foliage. It is regarded as one of David Austin's more robust, easy-care introductions, tolerating heat and humidity well, and it repeat-blooms generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Charles Darwin Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Charles Darwin's large, heavy blooms benefit from a sturdy, well-branched framework and occasional support after heavy rain.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001, Charles Darwin bears very large, deeply cupped blooms in a distinctive mustard-bronze to old-gold color that deepens as the flower ages, with a strong tea fragrance, on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its unusual bronze-gold tones set it apart from the more common clear yellows and pinks in the English rose palette, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: William Shakespeare 2000 Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; William Shakespeare 2000 replaced David Austin's earlier William Shakespeare introduction with a more disease-resistant plant carrying the same deep crimson color.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2000 as an improved replacement for his earlier William Shakespeare rose, this cultivar carries deep velvety crimson-purple, fully double blooms with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous shrub bred for markedly better disease resistance than the original 1987 introduction, which was notoriously prone to black spot. It repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading, and its dark, saturated color makes a dramatic accent among lighter companion plantings.
